title: OS Credential Dumping: NTDS
summary: NTDS targets the Active Directory database file held on Windows domain controllers, which contains password hashes and account information for every user and computer in the domain. Because the directory service keeps the file locked while running, the adversary copies it indirectly, using a volume shadow copy, a built-in directory maintenance utility, a raw disk read, or by locating a backup that already contains the same content. Domain administrator or equivalent rights are normally required, and the resulting hashes give very broad impersonation capability, so this is a late and high impact stage of an intrusion. Artefacts include shadow copy creation, unusual use of the directory utility, large reads or copies from the database folder, and access to backup media or files. Scheduled backup and approved recovery work produce similar evidence, so the reviewer must establish whether the activity fits a known maintenance window and account.

beginner.definition: NTDS is the main database file of Active Directory on a domain controller. It holds password hashes for domain accounts. This sub-technique means copying that database. It differs from the parent because the target is a whole domain, not a single computer.
beginner.whyItMatters: A domain controller holds credentials for the entire organisation. Copying this database can give an attacker thousands of accounts at once. The copy can be analysed elsewhere, without touching your network again. Detecting it early is one of the last chances before a full compromise. Legitimate backups create similar files, so context is essential.
howItWorks: A domain controller stores all domain account data in the NTDS file.
Windows locks that file, so it cannot simply be copied while running.
The attacker creates a shadow copy, which is a snapshot of the disk.
The database is taken from the snapshot, or an existing backup is located.
Sometimes a built-in directory tool is used to export the same data.
The copy is moved away and its password hashes are extracted later.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital where every ward door opens with one central master key. The key is never carried around; it stays in a locked office. A thief photographs the master key plan and takes the pictures home. Later, copies of that plan open every ward quietly. The NTDS file is that central plan, and one copy covers the whole hospital.
takeaways: The domain database is far more valuable to an attacker than a single host.
Shadow copies and backup access are the key artefacts to review.
Always check whether an approved backup explains the activity you see.

objectives: Explain what the Active Directory database contains and where it lives.
Describe why a domain controller file cannot be copied while the service runs.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the credential dumping parent.
Identify shadow copy and backup artefacts linked to directory database access.
Describe why domain wide hashes enable broad impersonation and movement.
